title: One sound, two spellings
instruction: Read blue and blew aloud. Both words share the exact same sequence of sounds despite playing completely different grammatical roles.
question: Which pair is homophonous?
explanation: The difference between blue and blew lies solely in spelling and meaning.

title: From an open vowel to a glide
example: The cap is under the cape.
instruction: Alternate cap and cape. Open your jaw for /æ/; for /eɪ/, glide the tongue upward towards a closer position.
question: In which word does the tongue position shift inside the syllable?
explanation: The vowel in cape is a diphthong in the reference profile.

title: Releasing the lips
example: Put the pin beside the bin.
instruction: Hold a hand close to your mouth. Compare the initial burst of air in pin with bin, and then with the p in spin.
question: Where is aspiration typically most noticeable?
explanation: Following /s/, the aspiration on /p/ is substantially reduced.

title: The hissing channel
example: Listen to the sip and the zip.
instruction: Hold the opening sound of sip and zip. Maintain the exact tongue groove and switch vocal fold vibration on and off.
question: Which onset is voiced?
explanation: /z/ shares the alveolar narrowing of /s/ while adding voicing.

title: Tongue tip and ridge
instruction: Alternate tap and dip. Feel the tongue tip sealing cleanly right behind the upper incisors.
question: What do /t/ and /d/ share?
explanation: Both close on the alveolar ridge; their release characteristics vary with context.

title: Shifting vowel height
example: Leave the pen on the seat.
instruction: Alternate seat and set. For set, drop the jaw and the body of the tongue slightly.
question: Which word has the higher vowel?
explanation: The contrast between /iː/ and /e/ depends on vowel quality and tongue height, not just length.

title: An unstressed neutral vowel
instruction: Say banana slowly and then at natural speed. Keep the central syllable prominent and relax the opening syllable completely.
question: Which vowel typically starts about?
explanation: The unstressed initial syllable takes a reduced central schwa vowel.

title: One contact, two voices
example: The fan is inside the van.
instruction: Say fan and van without altering the contact between upper teeth and lower lip. Hold the opening friction steady.
question: Which articulator touches the upper incisors?
explanation: Labiodental friction is produced between the lower lip and upper front teeth.

title: Closure at the back
example: Keep the coat beside the goat.
instruction: Alternate coat and goat. Keep the tongue tip relaxed and feel the closure made by the back of the tongue.
question: Where is the airway closed for /k/?
explanation: The back of the tongue rises against the soft palate to seal the airflow.

title: Three light onsets
instruction: Say hat, wet, and yes. Notice the glottal breath in h, the lip rounding in w, and the palatal raise in y.
question: Which onset uses lip rounding?
explanation: /w/ combines lip rounding with raising the back of the tongue.

title: A moving vowel
example: The kite is in the kit.
instruction: Alternate kite and kit. In kite, maintain a single smooth syllable pulse throughout the tongue glide.
question: Which word contains /aɪ/?
explanation: The diphthong glides upward towards a closer front position.

title: Friction versus stop-plus-friction
instruction: Lengthen the start of shoes. Then say choose and feel the brief firm stop before the friction begins.
question: Which onset begins with a complete closure?
explanation: The affricate /tʃ/ begins with a stop closure and releases into friction.

title: Central contact vs. approximation
instruction: Alternate right and light. For l, touch the ridge with the tip and let air pass around the sides; for r, leave a central gap.
question: Which onset releases air laterally?
explanation: /l/ directs airflow along the sides of the tongue.

title: Two vowels with written r
example: Park the cart in the square.
instruction: In Southern non-rhotic speech, hear cart and square without adding a consonant r at the end. The vowel in square varies across speakers.
question: Which comparison holds true?
solution: Written r need not produce a consonant sound
explanation: Realisation depends on accent variety and syllable position.

title: Three nasal closures
instruction: Cycle through the endings without adding a trailing vowel. Move the seal from lips, to tongue tip, to tongue back.
question: Which ending seals at the back of the tongue?
explanation: /ŋ/ combines velar closure with nasal airflow.

title: One written o, two vowels
example: Put the coat by the cot.
instruction: Compare coat and cot. Notice how lip rounding increases smoothly during the diphthong in coat.
question: Which word typically has /əʊ/?
explanation: In this reference accent, GOAT has a clear glide while LOT is a short monophthong.

title: Dental friction
instruction: Hold the opening sound of thin and then. Keep the tongue tip near the edge of the upper teeth and toggle voicing.
question: Which word starts with /ð/?
explanation: The opening sound of then is the voiced dental fricative.

title: Full, fool, and cup
instruction: Alternate full, fool, and cup. Contrast lip rounding and tongue height rather than lengthening every vowel.
question: Which word belongs to the FOOT lexical set?
explanation: Full uses the short /ʊ/ vowel in this reference.

title: Neutral vs. rounded lips
instruction: Hold the vowel of bird with relaxed lips. Round the lips firmly for the vowel of caught.
question: Which word uses the NURSE vowel?
explanation: /ɜː/ is central and typically unrounded.

title: Two glides from back or low
instruction: Compare boy and cow. In boy the tongue moves forward; in cow lip rounding increases towards the end.
question: Which word uses the CHOICE diphthong?
explanation: CHOICE glides upward towards /ɪ/.

title: Entering a cluster cleanly
instruction: Practise ring, then spring. Begin with steady /s/ hiss and move straight into the /p/ closure without adding an extra vowel before /s/.
question: How many syllables does spring have?
explanation: The initial three-consonant cluster shares a single vowel nucleus.

title: Holding the final consonant
example: The lamp fell off the desk.
instruction: Alternate lam and lamp. Prepare the final lip closure cleanly without adding an extra release vowel.
question: What distinguishes lamp from lam?
explanation: Final clusters maintain lexical contrast without adding a vowel.

title: Three plural endings
example: The cats, dogs and buses arrived.
instruction: Sort the endings when saying cats, dogs, and buses. Hear which word gains an extra syllable.
question: Which plural adds a syllable?
explanation: After a sibilant consonant, plural endings take /ɪz/.

title: Regular past tense endings
instruction: Compare the final syllable of waited against the crisp endings of packed and played.
question: Which past tense form adds a syllable?
explanation: After /t/ or /d/, regular past endings take /ɪd/.

title: Adjacent identical stops
instruction: Say black coat without inserting a vowel between the two /k/ sounds. Hold the closure slightly longer and release once.
question: What can the word boundary share?
explanation: Two adjacent stops at the same place of articulation normally share one hold phase.

title: Linking across vowels
instruction: Compare car in isolation with car is in non-rhotic speech. Listen for the linking r bridging smoothly into the next vowel.
question: Where can linking r appear?
explanation: A following vowel triggers linking r at the word boundary.

title: The prominent syllable
instruction: Tap once per syllable and give a firmer tap on the stressed syllable. Listen to changes in pitch and length.
question: Which syllable of banana takes primary stress?
explanation: The stress mark ˈ immediately precedes the prominent syllable.

title: Noun vs. verb stress shift
instruction: Read the verb first, then the noun. Practise shifting stress without changing the consonant order.
question: In which usage is the first syllable usually stressed?
explanation: Two-syllable noun/verb pairs frequently contrast initial vs. final stress.

title: Compound noun vs. phrase
example: A blackbird landed on a black board.
instruction: Contrast the bird species blackbird with a colour description. Emphasise the first element of the compound.
question: Which expression names a species?
explanation: Compounds commonly carry primary stress on their first component.

title: Locating stress in longer words
instruction: Break photographer into syllables and highlight -tog-. Notice how the unstressed vowels reduce around it.
question: Which syllable takes primary stress?
explanation: Photographer normally places primary stress on the second syllable.

title: Shifting stress in word families
example: Music and musicians filled the hall.
instruction: Compare music and musician. Keep the whole word smooth as the stressed syllable moves forward.
question: Which word stresses a later syllable?
explanation: Suffixes like -ian shift primary stress onto the preceding syllable.

title: One focus per tone group
instruction: Answer 'What did Maya book?' by highlighting room. Then repeat the sentence as an answer to 'Who booked a room?'
question: Which word do you highlight to answer 'Who?'
explanation: Nuclear stress shifts onto whichever item supplies the requested information.

title: Strong pronouns for contrast
instruction: Practise a neutral reading and then a reading contrasting him with her. Compare how clearly the vowels sound.
question: When is a strong form most likely?
explanation: Contrastive focus restores prominence to normally weak pronouns.

title: Light vs. strong auxiliaries
instruction: Practise can inside the sentence, then in the short reply 'Yes, we can.' Compare the vowel quality in both.
question: Where is the strong form of can expected?
explanation: Stranded or final auxiliaries retain their strong vowel.

title: Given vs. new information
instruction: Assume the listener already knows it is a scarf. Correct the colour by giving prominence to purple.
question: Which word carries the new information?
explanation: Prominence highlights what updates the shared context.

title: Moving a correction focus
instruction: Say the sentence to correct 'three', then say it again to correct 'coffees'. Shift only the focal word.
question: Where does the focus fall when correcting 'three'?
explanation: Corrective stress singles out the exact contrasted item.

title: Chunking an aside
instruction: Frame Sam with gentle boundaries to present it as parenthetical information. Compare with an unbroken reading.
question: Which element functions as the parenthetical aside?
explanation: Tone-unit phrasing sets off an aside from the core clause.

title: Structuring instructions
example: After lunch, take the blue bus.
instruction: Pause briefly after lunch, then keep 'take the blue bus' smoothly together as one unit.
question: Which chunk sets the time frame?
explanation: Clear phrasing boundaries make spoken instructions easier to process.

title: Contrasting two options
example: You take the stairs; I will take the lift.
instruction: Organise the sentence into two balanced groups, highlighting stairs and lift as opposing choices.
question: Which pair expresses the core contrast?
explanation: Those two nouns represent the explicitly contrasted alternatives.

title: Correcting a detail
instruction: Make the right day prominent while keeping the second part lighter as a foil. Avoid shouting the whole phrase.
question: Which word corrects Thursday?
explanation: Pitch movement pinpoints the corrected information.

title: Adding an afterthought
instruction: Deliver again as its own small trailing group. Then integrate it smoothly and notice the shift in attitude.
question: Which word delivers the added comment?
explanation: A separate tail group lets the comment carry its own emphasis.

title: Questions and speaker intent
instruction: Try both an open, friendly check and an insistent follow-up. Vary the final pitch movement.
question: What determines how the tune is interpreted?
explanation: Interrogative grammar does not lock a sentence into a single fixed contour.

title: Confirming a figure
instruction: Imagine you misheard the departure time. Place prominence on nine to request confirmation.
question: Which piece of information needs verification?
explanation: Echo prominence draws attention directly to the uncertain detail.

title: Leaving room for doubt
instruction: Try a decisive delivery and then a hesitant one. Notice how much the impression changes while the words stay identical.
question: What is needed to interpret attitude reliably?
explanation: An isolated pitch contour can convey multiple stances depending on context.

title: Tracking relative rise and fall
instruction: Trace a rise and then a fall with your hand while saying really in your own comfortable vocal register.
question: What is most useful to compare across voices?
explanation: Normalised relative contours allow fair comparison across different vocal ranges.

title: Buying thinking time
instruction: Leave a natural slight pause after well, as though gathering your thoughts before responding.
question: What can that brief pause signal?
explanation: Strategic pauses give speakers time to formulate ideas naturally.

title: Reducing function words
example: A cup of tea for Ben.
instruction: Say each word slowly first, then link 'cup of tea' smoothly. Hear how 'of' weakens.
question: Which word typically reduces here?
explanation: Unstressed function words routinely take weak forms in connected speech.

title: Quick polite offers
instruction: Practise slowly first, then join 'would you' smoothly across the boundary without losing clarity.
question: What must be preserved when speaking faster?
explanation: Natural reduction keeps the core message crisp and easy to follow.

title: Anticipating an upcoming closure
instruction: Say 'ten bikes' fluently. Notice how the lips prepare early for /b/, subtly shifting the preceding nasal.
question: Which sound influences the nasal?
explanation: Anticipatory lip closure can assimilate /n/ towards /m/.

title: Hearing connected word boundaries
instruction: Listen to the whole phrase before trying to separate words. Repeat smoothly without inserting silent gaps.
question: What helps segment fluent connected speech?
distractor: Expecting a pause after every word
explanation: In connected speech, word boundaries rarely contain physical silences.

title: Keeping a list open
example: We need paper, tape and string.
instruction: Deliver paper as an opening item and string as the final item. Contrast non-final continuation tunes with final closure.
question: Which item signals that the list continues?
distractor: string at the end of the list
explanation: List position and intonation work together to signal continuation vs. completion.

title: Closing a turn
instruction: Finish your turn with a calm fall and pause. Then try repeating as if about to add an exception.
question: What accompanies a turn-final tune?
explanation: Conversational turn-taking relies on several prosodic and timing cues together.

title: Routine check vs. surprise
instruction: Try the sentence first as a routine check, then with genuine surprise. Vary prominence and pitch range.
question: What stays identical across both deliveries?
explanation: Identical wording can express quite different pragmatic intentions.

title: Softening an opinion
instruction: Deliver the line firmly, then tentatively. Consider how a listener interprets confidence from the whole phrase.
question: What is the most informative check of attitude?
explanation: Perceived stance comes from the combined prosodic shape of the utterance.

title: Comfortable expressiveness
instruction: Repeat enthusiastically using your natural vocal range. Expand your relative pitch movement over brilliant.
question: What should you keep when imitating expressiveness?
distractor: Another speaker's exact pitch in Hz
explanation: Expressiveness transfers through relative movement rather than copying absolute pitch.

title: Noticing regional r
instruction: Compare a rhotic and a non-rhotic reading of farm. In rhotic varieties, an /r/ sound follows the vowel.
question: What difference is expected?
solution: Presence or absence of post-vocalic r
explanation: Both patterns occur naturally across different British and international accents.

title: Regional vowel splits
example: We took a bath after class.
instruction: Practise recognising bath with both a long back /ɑː/ and a short front /æ/. Notice the word remains unchanged.
question: What varies between those pronunciations?
explanation: Lexical vowel distribution differs between Southern and Northern British accents.

title: Variation in /t/
instruction: Listen to different speakers in your videos. In casual speech, a glottal stop may replace an alveolar /t/ in bottle.
question: What evidence tells you which variant was used?
explanation: Orthography does not predict which phonetic variant a speaker realises.

title: Recognising accepted variants
instruction: Listen to how different speakers open schedule. Compare realisations beginning with /ʃ/ versus /sk/.
question: How should a learner treat both pronunciations?
solution: Recognise both as the same word
explanation: Many words have more than one widely accepted standard pronunciation.

title: Prioritising meaning-bearing contrasts
example: Meet me at fifteen, not fifty.
instruction: Focus first on distinguishing the number endings and stress placement, then refine pauses and rhythm.
question: What should you secure first?
solution: That the listener understands the number
explanation: Clear lexical contrasts protect the core message of your utterance.
